oneSentence: A document symbol is the official code used to identify and retrieve a specific United Nations document, while prefixes such as A/RES/ show what kind of document it is and where it came from.
plainExplanation:
In the UN, many papers have an official identifier. That identifier is usually called a document symbol, or just a symbol. It works like a precise filing code, so people can find the exact text they need.

A symbol often contains parts that mean different things. For example, “A” usually points to the General Assembly, and “RES” points to a resolution. So “A/RES/…” is not a whole category by itself and not every document number looks like that. It is a common pattern inside a larger document symbol.

People also say document number, but that can be looser. In everyday use, some people use it as a synonym for document symbol. In stricter use, the symbol is the full official code, while the number may mean only the numeric part at the end.

What goes in is a document created in a UN body or process. The Secretariat or another responsible office assigns the official symbol using established conventions. What comes out is a standard reference that lets delegations, staff, researchers and the public search, cite and compare documents without relying only on titles, which may be long, similar or translated.

everydayAnalogy.title: A library shelf code for one report
everydayAnalogy.story: A translator receives a short field report and is told, “Please check the version filed under Cabinet 3, Shelf A, Folder 12.” That code is faster and more reliable than searching by a long title, especially if several reports have similar names. Another note says “Policy/Final” at the start of the code, which helps the translator recognise the type of document before opening it. The translator still needs the full code, not just the first part, to get the exact report.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A library shelf code usually points to a physical location, but a UN document symbol is not only about storage. It also reflects the issuing body and often the document category. In addition, UN symbols follow institutional conventions that can change across bodies and time, so they are more formal than an office filing label.

visual.title: How to read a UN document symbol
visual.learningObjective: After viewing this, a reader should be able to explain that a full symbol identifies one document, while parts such as A/RES/ give clues about body and document type.
visual.description: A left-to-right step diagram shows a document symbol being read in layers: full code first, then prefix, then body/type meaning, then the retrieval result. Read each box in order to see how the code narrows to one exact document.

steps.label: 1. Start with the full code
steps.explanation: Look for the entire identifier, not only one part of it. The full symbol is the safest way to search or cite a document.
steps.visualInstruction: Show a large sample code in a rounded rectangle, for example “A/RES/78/265”, with the whole code highlighted.

steps.label: 2. Notice the prefix
steps.explanation: A beginning segment such as “A/RES/” gives clues. It can signal both the UN body and the document category.
steps.visualInstruction: Visually split the sample into coloured segments: “A” | “RES” | “78/265”, with the prefix segment emphasised.

steps.label: 3. Read the clues carefully
steps.explanation: “A” commonly refers to the General Assembly, and “RES” commonly refers to a resolution. These clues help, but the full symbol is still needed for precision.
steps.visualInstruction: Add short callout labels above “A” saying “General Assembly” and above “RES” saying “resolution”.

steps.label: 4. Retrieve the exact text
steps.explanation: Using the complete symbol lets you find the right document, even when titles are similar, translated differently or reused across years.
steps.visualInstruction: Show an arrow from the full code to a document card titled “Exact document found”, with a smaller note “do not rely on title alone”.

visual.interaction: On hover or tap, each segment reveals a short tooltip explaining what that part commonly indicates; keyboard focus shows the same tooltips in order.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram explains how to read a UN document symbol in four steps. First, use the full code, for example A slash RES slash 78 slash 265, because the complete identifier is the safest way to search. Second, notice that the beginning part, such as A slash RES slash, is only part of the symbol. Third, read the clues in that prefix: A commonly points to the General Assembly and RES commonly points to a resolution. Fourth, use the full symbol to retrieve the exact document, because titles alone may be similar, translated or repeated.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static four-panel diagram shows the full sample code, then its split parts, then labels for body and document type, then an exact document result card. No animation is used; colour and arrows show the reading order.

workedExample.scenario: A student is trying to locate a General Assembly resolution mentioned in a briefing note.
process: The student copies the full symbol rather than searching only the resolution title.
The student recognises “A” as the General Assembly and “RES” as a resolution, so the citation format makes sense.
The student enters the full code in the UN document search system.
The system returns the exact resolution record, including the official text and related metadata.
workedExample.result: The student finds the correct document quickly and avoids confusing it with another text on a similar topic from a different year or body.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A policy officer in a Permanent Mission is searching past General Assembly resolutions for agreed language on AI governance and wants to trace exact wording across sessions.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Knowing how document symbols work helps the officer retrieve the correct records, compare versions and cite earlier texts accurately in draft instructions or speaking points.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Use approved internal systems and normal information-handling rules; do not paste unpublished negotiating text or sensitive internal comments into an unapproved public AI service.

whyItMatters: If you cannot tell one UN document from another, it is easy to quote the wrong text, miss a previous decision or misunderstand where a proposal stands. A document symbol helps you verify source, body and document type before you rely on a document. For non-specialists, that matters because debates on AI, peace and security, development or human rights often refer to earlier UN texts by symbol rather than by full title. Reading the symbol correctly improves traceability: you can find the authoritative document, check whether it is a draft or an adopted text, and avoid mixing up a resolution with a report, letter or meeting record.

commonMisconceptions.correction: It is usually only a prefix pattern inside a larger document symbol. It tells you useful things about source and type, but you normally still need the rest of the code to identify one exact document.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A document symbol and a resolution are the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: A resolution is a kind of document or decision text. A document symbol is the official identifier used to find and cite that text. Many other document types also have symbols, including reports and letters.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The title of a UN document is enough for searching.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Titles can be long, similar, translated or reused across years and bodies. The symbol is more precise because it is designed to point to one specific record.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: It is the UN’s official filing code for a document. Parts of the code can hint at the issuing body and document type, but the full code is what lets you find the exact text.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: A UN document symbol is a structured identifier assigned under UN documentation conventions to support retrieval, citation and record control. In many cases it contains segments that indicate the principal organ or issuing body and the document category. For example, the pattern A/RES/ commonly signals a General Assembly resolution, but that prefix is not by itself the complete identifier. The full symbol, including its later elements, distinguishes one document from others. “Document number” is often used informally as a synonym, though some users reserve “number” for only the numeric component. The term should also be distinguished from the underlying document type: a resolution, report or letter may each have a symbol, but the symbol is the reference code, not the substance or legal effect of the document.

keyTakeaway: The symbol is the UN document’s exact reference code; prefixes such as A/RES/ give clues, but the full symbol is what identifies the right text.

quickCheck.question: What does “A/RES/” most usefully tell you?
options: It is the complete identifier for one exact UN document.
It is a prefix that commonly signals a General Assembly resolution, but you still need the full symbol.
It proves the text was adopted by consensus.
It is the title of a UN database.
quickCheck.explanation: “A/RES/” is commonly a meaningful prefix, not the whole reference. It helps you recognise body and document type, but the remaining parts of the symbol are needed to identify the exact document.
